prompt.context: A luxury car company offers an option to include a top-of-the-line stereo system in their cars. The stereo unit is operated as a separate P&L within the car company.
prompt.question: Profits for the stereo unit are lower than their competitors. Why might this be, and what should the client do about it?

clarifying_info.q: How is the radio sold to customers?
clarifying_info.a: It is sold as an upgraded feature offered at the dealership when the car is sold.

clarifying_info.q: How does the radio compare to competitors in terms of quality and features?
clarifying_info.a: The radio's quality and features are in line with that of competitors.

clarifying_info.q: Can the company use different dealers or expand geographically?
clarifying_info.a: All sales are handled by the same national dealership. There is no option to switch to other dealers or expand geographically.

clarifying_info.q: What is the price of the radio?
What are the variable costs per unit?
clarifying_info.a: Total variable cost per unit is $500. Fixed costs don't matter for this analysis.

clarifying_info.q: How are salespeople at the dealership compensated for selling the radio?
clarifying_info.a: Salespeople at the dealership are provided with a commission. Ask the interviewer for the specific commission rate if needed.

clarifying_info.q: Are there differences in brand awareness or geographic factors versus competitors?
clarifying_info.a: No differences in brand awareness or geographic location explain the gap.

exhibits.title: Pricing Study – Projected Sales by Price
exhibits.shows: A chart showing projected sales volume (y-axis, units ranging roughly 50–170) at four price points: $1,000, $1,500, $2,000, and $2,500.

exhibits.title: Radio Sales by Commission per Dealer
exhibits.shows: A chart showing radio sales volume (y-axis, units ranging roughly 50–170) at four commission levels: 10%, 15%, 20%, and 25%.

framework: Profit Model: Decompose into revenue and costs – assess whether the issue is pricing, volume, or variable costs
Variable Costs: Explore parts, manufacturing, distribution; VC per unit = $500
Pricing: Current price = $1,500; examine price sensitivity using Exhibit 1
Sales Channel: How is the radio sold? Who markets/advertises it? How are salespeople compensated (commission structure)?
Customers: Luxury car buyers – consider their price sensitivity
Competition: Product quality and pricing are comparable to competitors; geography/brand awareness are not differentiating factors here

questions.prompt: Question 1: Walk through your framework for diagnosing why profits are lower than competitors.
questions.guidance: A strong answer covers: (1) profit model – revenue vs. cost drivers; (2) variable costs per unit; (3) pricing and price sensitivity; (4) sales channel and commission structure; (5) customer profile. Candidate should quickly identify that VC=$500 and price=$1,500, giving a $1,000 gross margin per unit, and then probe volume as the likely issue. They should probe how salespeople are incentivized.

questions.prompt: Question 2: What do you make of Exhibit 1 (Pricing Study)?
questions.guidance: Key insight: Although sales volume changes with price, the drop is not dramatic – luxury car buyers are relatively price-insensitive. Raising the price from $1,500 toward $2,000 or $2,500 is a viable lever to increase profit per unit. However, the client also wants to increase volume, so the candidate should not stop at price and should brainstorm other levers.

steps: Even with fewer units sold at $2,000, total contribution is higher – confirming low price sensitivity
math.answer: Raising price increases total profit despite lower volume; customers are not very price-sensitive.

questions.prompt: Question 3: Why aren't radios selling at the same volume as competitors? What can the client do to increase volume?
questions.guidance: Candidate should return to framework / value chain. Key insight: radios are sold by dealership salespeople on commission. If the commission is low, salespeople have little incentive to push the radio upgrade. Providing Exhibit 2 shows the relationship between commission rate and volume. Strong candidates identify this as a 'push' marketing problem – salespeople will actively promote the radio only if the commission makes it worth their time. Extra credit for naming this 'push marketing' and for suggesting pull marketing alternatives.

questions.prompt: Question 4: If we increase commissions, how much will profit change? Run the math.
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a simple table across commission levels using the volume data from Exhibit 2. They should find that increasing commissions from 10% to 20% increases total margin despite lower per-unit margin.

math.setup: Price = $1,500; VC = $500. Commission = % × Price. Per-unit margin = Price – VC – Commission. Total margin = Volume × Per-unit margin.
math.answer: Total margin is maximized at 20% commission ($63,000). Beyond 20%, volume gains are not enough to offset the per-unit margin reduction.

brainstorming.prompt: Aside from raising commissions and raising price, what other creative ideas could help the client increase volume or profitability?

categories.name: Pull Marketing
ideas: Invest in advertising the radio directly to luxury car buyers before they visit the dealership
Create in-store displays or test-listening stations at dealerships
Use digital marketing targeting luxury vehicle shoppers

categories.name: Partnerships
ideas: Partner with high-end audio brands (e.g., Bang & Olufsen, Bose) to co-brand the radio
Partner with XM/SiriusXM satellite radio to bundle a subscription and increase perceived value

categories.name: Bundling & Packaging
ideas: Bundle the radio with other luxury add-ons as a 'premium package'
Offer financing for add-ons to reduce sticker-price sensitivity

categories.name: Competitive Response Awareness
ideas: Consider whether raising prices or commissions could prompt competitors to undercut
Monitor competitor commission structures to stay competitive

recommendation: Increase the dealership commission rate to 20% to maximize total profit ($63,000 vs. current $59,500 at 10%), leveraging the strong relationship between commission and sales volume
Consider raising the radio price toward $2,000, as luxury car buyers are relatively price-insensitive, and the higher per-unit margin offsets volume loss
risks: Competitors may respond to a price increase by undercutting, eroding volume
Higher commissions could be copied by competitors, raising industry-wide cost structures
Over-reliance on push marketing through salespeople may be fragile if dealership incentives change
next_steps: Pilot the 20% commission structure at select dealerships and measure volume uplift
Explore pull marketing initiatives (advertising, brand partnerships) to complement the push strategy
Evaluate a modest price increase test ($1,750–$2,000) with a controlled group of dealerships
